body.text: Why does Central Bank of Somalia still shape capital allocation and market pricing across global desks? Behind the headline numbers lies a structural mechanism that quietly governs liquidity, risk, and long-term purchasing power.

The Central Bank of Somalia (CBS, Somali: Bankiga Dhexe ee Soomaaliya, Arabic: البنك المركزي الصومالي) is the central bank and monetary authority of the Federal Republic of Somalia. It is headquartered in Mogadishu.

Under its statutory mandate, the bank is responsible for price and financial stability, monetary and foreign-exchange policy, currency issuance, management of foreign reserves, supervision of financial institutions, and oversight of payment and settlement systems.
It also acts as banker, adviser and fiscal agent to the Federal Government of Somalia and the Federal Member States, and publishes monetary, financial and economic statistics.

body.text: The institution was established as the Somali National Bank after independence in 1960 and was renamed the Central Bank of Somalia in 1975. Its operations were suspended after the collapse of the central government in 1991.
Efforts to restore the institution began during the transitional-government period, and its statutory position was re-established by the Central Bank of Somalia Act 2012.

Since its re-establishment, the CBS has introduced regulatory, supervisory and payment-system reforms. These have included licensing frameworks for banks and non-bank financial institutions, interbank clearing and settlement infrastructure, bank-account and payment-code standards, and systems for instant payments.

Reports by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Bank and African Development Bank have examined these reforms as part of Somalia’s wider programme of financial and public-sector reconstruction.
History
Pre-independence monetary institutions

The institutional origins of central banking in Somalia date to the Italian Trusteeship Administration. In 1950, the Cassa per la Circolazione Monetaria della Somalia (CCMS) was created to issue and regulate currency in the Trust Territory of Somaliland. The CCMS introduced the somalo in the same year.

In the British Somaliland Protectorate, the Indian rupee remained in circulation until 1951, when it was replaced by the East African shilling. The CCMS moved its headquarters from Rome to Mogadishu in 1959.
Somali National Bank, 1960, 1975

The Somali National Bank was established in 1960, following the independence and union of the former British and Italian-administered territories. Its responsibilities included monetary stability, regulation of banking and credit, management of external reserves, and service as fiscal agent to the government.

A presidential decree issued in 1961 provided for the replacement of the East African shilling in northern Somalia by the Somali shilling. The bank issued the first Somali-shilling banknotes in 1962, and the assets of the CCMS were transferred to it in 1963.
The Somali Credit Bank was merged into the Somali National Bank in 1968. During this period, the institution carried out both central-banking and commercial-banking functions.
Central Bank of Somalia, 1975, 1991

In 1975, the Somali National Bank was renamed the Central Bank of Somalia. The change was associated with a move towards a more distinct central-banking mandate covering monetary policy, currency management and oversight of the financial sector.

During the 1980s, Somalia faced rising external debt, weak export performance and economic stagnation. The government entered structural-adjustment programmes with the IMF and World Bank. Armed conflict and the breakdown of state institutions intensified towards the end of the decade. The CBS suspended operations after the collapse of the central government in January 1991.
Institutional disruption and restoration

The absence of an operational central monetary authority after 1991 contributed to widespread use of foreign currency, irregular production of Somali-shilling banknotes and the growth of privately operated financial services, particularly money-transfer businesses.

Institutional restoration began during the transitional-government period. Mohamed Mohamud Ulusow served as governor from 2001 to 2005, followed by Bashir Isse Ali from 2005 to 2010 and Abdullahi Haji Jama from 2010 to 2013. The Central Bank of Somalia Act 2012 re-established the bank’s statutory role as the national monetary authority.
Reform since 2012

Following Somalia’s transition from the Transitional Federal Government to the permanent Federal Government of Somalia in 2012, the Central Bank of Somalia gradually resumed its administrative, regulatory, and operational functions. Early reforms included restoration of international banking links, installation of a core banking system, development of fiscal-agent services, and the initial rebuilding of banking supervision.
These measures provided the institutional basis for reforms undertaken from 2019 onwards.
Reforms since 2019

Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi was appointed Governor of the Central Bank of Somalia in April 2019. During his tenure, the CBS implemented institutional and financial-sector reforms aimed at strengthening governance, regulatory and supervisory frameworks, and operational capacity.

These reforms included the adoption of a function-based organisational structure in 2019, with clearly defined reporting lines, job descriptions, and performance objectives. The bank introduced merit-based recruitment, annual staff appraisals and training plans, while recruitment was moved towards competitive selection.

The CBS also expanded its role as fiscal agent to the federal government. Connections between the bank’s systems and the Somalia Financial Management Information System were established in 2019, allowing government revenues and payments to be processed electronically.
Federal employees, security personnel and suppliers were subsequently paid directly into their accounts, while the Ministry of Finance gained direct access to government account balances at the CBS.

Financial-sector supervision was extended during the same period. Regulations governing mobile-money operators were issued in 2019, licensing began in 2020, and four operators had been licensed by 2023. The bank also continued the licensing and supervision of commercial banks and money-transfer businesses and introduced monthly reporting requirements for licensed mobile-money operators.

Development of the National Payment System began in 2019 with World Bank assistance. The system connected licensed commercial banks through clearing and settlement infrastructure managed by the CBS. Its implementation required a private fibre-optic network, disaster-recovery facilities and upgrades to commercial banks’ core systems.
The platform entered operation in 2021, and the national quick-response standard, SOMQR, was introduced in 2023.

Internal operations and financial controls were also revised. The bank automated accounting and operational processes, developed internal policies and procedures, expanded its research and statistical functions, and began publishing quarterly economic reports. The report linked stronger internal controls to repeated clean external-audit opinions.

The report also identified unfinished reforms. These included widening the regulatory perimeter, strengthening the bank’s operational and financial independence, completing amendments to financial-sector legislation, and establishing a sustainable funding model. It noted that the CBS remained dependent on commissions from federal-government revenue and required adequate capitalisation to support a more independent revenue base.
Mandate and governance
The primary statutory objective of the CBS is to achieve and maintain domestic price stability.

Its other functions include supporting financial-system stability, formulating and implementing monetary and foreign-exchange policy, issuing and managing currency, managing foreign reserves, licensing and supervising financial institutions, overseeing payment and settlement systems, serving as banker and fiscal agent to government, and publishing financial and economic statistics.

The bank is governed by a board of directors and headed by a governor. Its internal arrangements include committees responsible for decision-making, risk management, audit and other control functions. IMF programme reviews have reported the continued implementation of safeguards recommendations and changes to governance and decision-making procedures.
Legal status and accountability

The Central Bank of Somalia Act 2012 establishes the CBS as an autonomous legal entity. The Act provides for legal personality, a head office and branches, authorised capital, exemption from taxation, and powers to issue regulations. It also sets out the bank’s relationship with Parliament, the government and other public entities.

The Act requires the bank to publish annual reports, financial statements, monetary-policy statements and other reports. It generally prohibits lending to government and public entities, while permitting temporary direct advances subject to statutory conditions. The bank also serves as fiscal agent, banker and foreign-exchange dealer for the government.
Board and executive management

The Act assigns the general management of the bank to a board of directors and provides for a governor and deputy governor. It addresses the composition and appointment of the board, eligibility and disqualification, meetings, remuneration, confidentiality, and the powers of the board.
The governor and deputy governor are appointed under the statutory procedure set out in the Act.

The bank’s published organisational structure groups its work under currency and banking operations, monetary, financial and regulatory policy, financial, administrative and support services, the Office of the Governor, and internal audit. The CBS website also publishes separate pages for the board of directors and senior management.
